label: Claude Haiku 5.5
output:
**Rating: 4 out of 5 stars**

We are a Lutheran congregation in Minneapolis with a nave about 92 feet long. Since 2020 we had livestreamed worship with a webcam mounted on a shelf, and it did the job poorly. Last winter we bought the Lindqvist Optics PT-20 through Chancel AV for $2,140, plus $95 for a wall mount. I'm writing this because other small churches will weigh the cost the way we did, and I'd rather they hear what it did and didn't do for us.

**Setup.** We mounted the camera on the balcony rail at the back of the nave and run one PoE cable up to it, so there's no separate power brick at the top of the stairs. The camera feeds an old office PC running OBS, which streams to our YouTube channel. The camera offers NDI HX and plain HDMI out. We use the NDI route. It's been dependable, but I'd want a volunteer who can handle a bit of software, because the video reaches the stream only through OBS. Expect a half day to get the scenes and presets sorted the first time.

We stored nine presets: altar, pulpit, lectern, font, choir loft, piano, a wide shot, and two for the chancel steps. Erik, our sixteen-year-old acolyte, runs the camera from the free web app on a tablet. He learned it in one afternoon. Most Sundays one person switches between presets during the service, and it's manageable.

**Picture quality.** In ordinary light the picture is clear at 1080p60. The 20x optical zoom lets us frame the lectern closely without a cropped digital image, which the old webcam could never do. Close-ups of the pulpit and the font look natural. The wide shot is good enough for the back pews to see the whole room.

The camera is not a miracle in dim light. At our Easter Vigil in April, a candlelight service where we sang "Christ the Lord Is Risen Today" with only candles, the picture got grainy. It stayed usable, though, and the old webcam showed almost nothing but dots. If your worship is mostly in low light, budget for better lighting too, and test the camera in the room at the hour you'll actually use it.

**What it fixed.** The most important change is for people who can't be in the pews. Delores, who is 82 and homebound, called after the first Sunday with the new camera to say she could finally read the hymn numbers on the board. Hearing that made the purchase feel worth it to me. For many of our online viewers, who usually number 30 to 60 on a Sunday, the difference is that they can now see the altar and the faces of the people leading worship.

**What it didn't fix, and some problems.** The first Sunday, the presets had drifted a few degrees by the time of the sermon. Firmware 2.4, released in March, corrected that, and we haven't had the problem since. Ask your supplier about firmware before you install.

Autofocus hunts when someone walks between the camera and the pulpit. We now lock focus on each preset, which works, but it's one more step to remember.

The printed manual is thin, and the translation is rough in places. We relied on Chancel AV's technical support. Marcy on their support line was excellent on the phone, and I'd count that as part of what you're paying for.

Please understand this clearly: **the camera did nothing for our sound problem.** Our audio was poor before and it's still poor. Audio is not the camera's job. If your sound is bad, the money for a microphone system and a proper mixer will do more for your online congregation than the camera will. We learned that the hard way.

**Would I buy it again?** Yes, for what we needed, which was a camera that could show the whole room, zoom in on the people and places that matter, and be run by a volunteer. But I'd be honest that a congregation under about 100 might do fine with something cheaper. We have a good reason to want the zoom and the presets, and our room is long. If your room is small and your viewers mostly watch from the sanctuary's front rows, a less expensive camera might serve you well. Ask yourself what problem you're solving before you spend the money.

So, four stars. The camera is well made and it solved the problem we bought it for. It is not a complete livestream system, and it doesn't fix sound or light. Budget for those too.

Pastor, Lutheran congregation, Minneapolis, Minnesota
